45.-(7)
Order
excluding media representatives or prohibiting publication –

The court may
make an order,

.  .  .

(c) prohibiting the publication of a report of the hearing or a
specified part of the hearing,

Where the court
is of the opinion that … publication of the report, …, would cause emotional
harm to a child who is a witness at or a participant in the hearing or is the
subject of the proceeding.

(8)
Prohibition:
identifying child. –
No person shall publish or make public information
that has the effect of identifying a child who is a witness at or a participant
in a hearing or the subject or a proceeding, or the child’s parent or foster
parent or a member of the child’s family.

(9)
Idem:
order re adult. –
The court may make an order prohibiting the publication
of information that has the effect of identifying a person charged with an
offence under this Part.

.  .  .

85. – (3)
Idem

– a person who contravenes subsection 45(8) or 76(11) (publication of
identifying information) or an order prohibiting publication made under clause
45(7)(c) or subsection 45(9), and a director, officer, or employee of a
corporation who authorizes, permits or concurs in such a contravention by the
corporation, is guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to a fine of
not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than three
years, or to both.

HEARD:

MESBUR J.

REASONS FOR DECISION

Nature of the appeal:

[
1
]

After a nine-day hearing in the Ontario Court of Justice in the
spring of 2009, Waldman J made the three children who are the subject of this
appeal Crown Wards with no access for the purpose of adoption.  Their
grandmother appeals from that disposition.  The children had been in the care
of the grandmother and grandfather, and were apprehended from their care by the
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto (CCAST) in April of 2007.  The
children have been in foster care since then.

[
2
]

The grandmother alleges the trial judge made various errors.  The
first she characterizes as “errors of fact”.  In this regard, she says the
trial judge’s reasons are unsupported by the facts and the evidence given.  She
also says the trial judge placed undue weight on “the relationship between the
foster parents as against the relationship between the appellant and the
children.”

[
3
]

The grandmother also advances the following additional grounds for
appeal:

(a)

Failure to properly evaluate the method adopted by Dr. Betty
Kershner in conducting parenting capacity assessment … [she] did not contact or
interview collaterals and relied mainly on the information obtained from the
CCAS to arrive at her conclusions;

(b)

Dismissive nature of the other expert reports;

(c)

Dismissive nature of the video testimony of the oldest of the
children, T.C.;

(d)

Misapprehension and misapplication of the videotape evidence;

(e)

Non-recognition of the inconsistent evidence of Ms. Munoz as regards
the assault allegation/charge;

(f)

The participation of the adoptive/foster parent in the proceeding
violated the rights of the Appellants in Appeal to have a hearing which was
free from bias and interference;

(g)

The fact that the adoptive/foster parent was in attendance and was
permitted to give evidence at the proceedings violated the right of the
Appellant to have a hearing in the absence of the public;

(h)

The judgment placed the onus of not being involved in the children’s
life on the appellants (against the preponderance of evidence) as opposed to
the respondent;

(i)

The characterization by the trial judge of the appellants as
intellectually and emotionally limited clearly violates the principles of
fundamental justice under section 15 of the
Charter
;

(j)

The denial of custody and/or access to the appellants constitute a
breach of their fundamental rights under section 7 of the
Charter
;

(k)

The assessments and comments of the trial judge on the appellants
were deprecatory and violated their rights under section 12 of the
Charter;

(l)

The failure to consider that the appellants had de facto custody of
the children for almost three years, and primary care of the children for
almost two years prior to their apprehension;

(m)

The failure to properly consider that the CCAST
gave a tacit approval for permanent placement of the children with the
appellant prior to the trial as well as their active participation and completion
of parenting classes.

The standard of review:

[
4
]

The alleged errors on the part of the trial judge can be
characterized as either mistakes of fact, or mistakes of mixed fact and law.
As a result, they can only be overturned if the trial judge made what is
described as an “overriding and palpable error”.

[
5
]

This is because factual findings made by a trial judge are entitled
to significant deference on appeal.  An appeal court should only reverse them
if the trial judge has made a “palpable and overriding error”.  A palpable
error is one that is plainly seen on the face of the record.
[1]
If there is an
indication the trial judge did not consider relevant factors or evidence, this
may show she did not properly weigh all the factors.  Then the appellate court
may review the trial evidence, to determine if the trial judge ignored or
misdirected herself with respect to the evidence.  An omission is only a
material error “if it gives rise to the reasoned belief that the trial judge
must have forgotten, ignored or misconceived the evidence in a way that
affected his conclusion.”
[2]

It is important to remember, however, that unless there is a clear error on the
face of the record, an appeal court is not entitled to substitute its own views
for the trial judge’s, merely because it would have weighed the evidence
differently and arrived at another result.
[3]

The legal framework:

[
6
]

The trial was a Status Review Application.  The only issue on such
an application is disposition.  The test on disposition is what is in the best
interests of the children, using the criteria in section 37(3) of the
CFSA
,
which are enumerated as follows:

1.

The child’s physical, mental and emotional
needs, and the appropriate care or treatment to meet those needs.

2.

The child’s physical, mental and emotional level
of development.

3.

The child’s cultural background.

4.

The religious faith, if any, in which the child
is being raised.

5.

The importance for the child’s development of a
positive relationship with a parent and a secure place as a member of a family.

6.

The child’s relationships and emotional ties to
a parent, sibling, relative, other member of the child’s extended family or
member of the child’s community.

7.

The importance of continuity in the child’s care
and the possible effect on the child of disruption of that continuity.

8.

The merits of a plan for the child’s care
proposed by a society, including a proposal that the child be placed for
adoption or adopted, compared with the merits of the child remaining with or
returning to a parent.

9.

The child’s views and wishes, if they can be
reasonably ascertained.

10.

The effect on the child of delay in the disposition of the case.

11.

The risk that the child may suffer harm through being removed from,
kept away from, returned to or allowed to remain in the care of a parent.

12.

The degree of risk, if any, that justified the finding that the
child is in need of protection.

13.

Any other relevant circumstance.

[
7
]

In determining a child’s best interests, the court must consider the
degree of risk from the point of view of the child.  Justice Sherr in
Jewish
Child and Family Services v. R.K.
[4]

put it this way:

The significance of the
child-centred approach is that good intentions are not enough.  The test is not
whether the parents have seen the light and intend to change, but whether they
have in fact changed and are now able to give the child the care that is in his
best interests. There is not to be experimentation with a child’s life ...
There has to be some demonstrated basis for a determination that the parents
are able to parent the child without endangering his safety.

[
8
]

Once a child is made a Crown Ward, any
access order in relation to the child is automatically terminated.  If access
is to be ordered, the person seeking access bears the onus under section 59 of
satisfying the court that the relationship between that person and the child is
beneficial and meaningful to the child
and
that access will not impair a
child’s future opportunities for adoption.

A brief history of the involvement of the Catholic
Children’s Aid Society:

[
9
]

The trial judge set out in some detail the history of the children,
their grandparents, the involvement of the CCAST and the children’s
apprehension from their grandparents’ care.  I will only set out a very brief
outline of the facts in order to give some context to my reasons.

[
10
]

V.L. is the appellant’s daughter.  V.L. is now
28 years old, and is the mother of all three of the children who are the
subject of this appeal.  The eldest child, T.C., is now 8.  Her brother D.L.1
is 7, and the youngest brother D.L.2 will be 6 next month.

[
11
]

V.L. lived at home with her parents, E.L. and W.L.
when each of the children was born.  She began to leave the children with her
parents more and more, while she went out.  Often she would be away for days at
a time, essentially abandoning the children.  Eventually, her parents contacted
the CCAST, who became involved with the family in around 2005.

[
12
]

The children had effectively lived with their
grandparents since birth.  The grandparents were prepared to continue to care
for them.  After conducting an assessment of the grandparents’ home, the CCAST
entered into a voluntary placement where the children were placed in the
grandparents’ care, subject to a supervision order.  The Society supervised the
children in the home for about eighteen months.  They provided the grandparents
with the assistance of parental support workers to assist them in the
challenging task of caring for these three small rambunctious children.

[
13
]

By sometime in 2007 the Society was prepared to
recommend that the children be placed with the grandparents, and the Society’s
involvement with the family end. They were in the process of proceeding with a
Status Review Application seeking termination of their involvement, and the
grandparents obtaining custody of the three children.  Before that happened,
however, an incident occurred in April of 2007, that changed that plan.

[
14
]

The Society received a call from a member of the
public, reporting that a woman had been seen on the street beating a small
child.  The witness apparently tried to intervene, but was unable to assist.
The Society and the police investigated.  The grandmother was identified as the
woman who had assaulted the child.  She was charged, and eventually entered a
guilty plea to the charges.  She was placed on probation.  The children were
apprehended, and the Society placed them in a foster home, where they remain to
this day.

[
15
]

Since the children were apprehended, the CCAST
has made arrangements for the children to have access visits with their
grandparents.  This access has been supervised by the Society.  The Society has
monitored the children in the home of the foster parents.  They obtained
psychological assessments of the children shortly after their apprehension and
again about sixteen months ago.  They also commissioned a parenting capacity
assessment of the grandparents to assist in determining what would be best for
the children, and the capacity of the grandparents to meet their needs.   The
parenting capacity assessment was done on the consent of all parties.

[
16
]

At the trial last summer, the Society requested
an order making the children Crown Wards with no access, so that they could be
adopted.  Their foster family is apparently interested in adopting all three
children.  The trial judge agreed, and made that order.  The grandmother
appeals, and says the children should be returned to her care.

The trial judge’s reasons:

[
17
]

In lengthy, careful and comprehensive reasons,
the trial judge articulated the law that governs the type of orders that are
available to the court.
[5]

First, the court must consider less disruptive alternatives than removing a
child from the care of the persons who had charge of the child immediately
before the society’s intervention, unless these alternatives would be
inadequate to protect the child.

[
18
]

The court is required to look at community
placements, including family members, before deciding to place a child in care.

[
19
]

In determining the appropriate disposition, the
court must decide what is in the child’s best interests, using the criteria set
out in section 37(3) of the
Child and Family Services Act
(
CFSA
)
.

[
20
]

The trial judge noted that since the children
had all been found to be children in need of protection, at the status hearing
before her, she had to determine two things.  First, she had to determine
whether the children should be returned to the caregiver from whom they were
apprehended, that is, the grandparents, or, given the time they had been in
care, whether they should be made Crown Wards.  In coming to the determination,
the court must determine the children’s best interests according to the
criteria in s. 37(3) of the
CFSA.

[
21
]

Second, if the trial judge decided the children
should be made Crown Wards, she would have to decide if the grandparents should
have access to the children.  She recognized that on this issue, the onus would
be the grandparents to show two things.  First, they would have to show the
relationship between them and the children was beneficial to the children, and
second, they would have to show that access would not impair the children’s
future opportunity for adoption.
[6]

[
22
]

The appellant takes no issue with the trial
judge’s articulation of the legal framework governing this case.

[
23
]

The trial judge heard from a number of
witnesses.  On the issue of the assault of April 2007 she heard from Ms. Munoz,
who had actually witnessed the assault.  The trial judge also viewed the videotaped
evidence of T.C., taken by a police officer and a social worker a day or so
after the occurrence.  At the time of this interview, T.C. had just turned 5.

[
24
]

The trial judge also heard from the grandmother
and the grandfather about this incident.  Although the grandmother had pleaded
guilty to the assault, at the status review hearing she completely denied that
the incident occurred.  This contradicted, in large part, the grandmother’s own
evidence in an earlier affidavit in which she admitted to an “error in
judgment” that she “publicly exhibited” on the day in question.

[
25
]

Having heard all the evidence, the trial judge
determined that the evidence of the independent eye witness was “clear,
consistent, objective and detailed.”  She accepted that evidence, and did not
accept the grandmother’s.  Those conclusions are overwhelmingly supported by
the evidence.  There is no basis on which to interfere with that finding.  As a
result, the trial judge concluded that the grandmother had indeed assaulted the
child, and accepted Ms. Munoz’ description of the event.

[
26
]

The trial judge was clear, however, that even
though she believed grandmother had assaulted the child, that fact alone was
not sufficient to support an order of Crown Wardship.  She properly stated that
it was but one example of the grandmother’s parenting ability, which had to be
considered along with all the rest of the evidence at trial.

[
27
]

The trial judge then considered the parenting
capacity assessment conducted by Dr. Betty Kershner.  The assessment had been
commissioned on consent of the CCAST and the grandparents.  The trial judge
found Dr. Kershner’s evidence thoughtful and helpful.  The trial judge
carefully analysed both Dr. Kershner’s methodology and conclusions.  Again, the
trial judge was clear that the parenting capacity assessment was not of itself
determinative of the issues before the court.  As the trial judge put it at
paragraph 26 of her reasons, “insofar as [the parenting capacity assessment] is
consistent with the balance of the evidence, it can provide the court with a
deeper understanding of the people assessed.”

[
28
]

Dr. Kershner was very critical of the
grandparents’ interaction with the children, and the behaviour they exhibited
during the observed access visits.  She noted grandfather’s favouritism toward
his granddaughter as well as his humiliation of D.L.1.  Dr. Kershner concluded
that the grandparents were not in tune with the children, their expectations of
the children were not age-appropriate, and they created a stressful,
uncomfortable atmosphere for the children.

[
29
]

Dr. Kershner opined that both the grandmother
and grandmother functioned cognitively in the “borderline range”.  She viewed
the grandmother as having a borderline personality disorder, which she
described as “antisocial personality disorder and paranoid personality
disorder”.  She commented on the grandmother’s rages.  Although Dr. Kershner
recognized that the grandmother would be able to meet the children’s
“instrumental needs”, she would not be capable of meeting the children's
social, educational and developmental needs.

[
30
]

As the trial judge put it, Dr. Kershner
concluded that “the grandparents are not capable of parenting the children, are
not open to and will not benefit from supports to assist them in gaining
insight, developing better parenting skills or changing their parenting
behaviour.    She found that the grandparents were not capable of meeting the children’s
psychological, social, medical or academic needs.”
[7]

[
31
]

The trial judge pointed out that Dr. Kershner’s
observations were consistent with the observations and evidence of other access
supervisors, the society social workers, and case aids. The trial judge herself
observed that the grandfather lacked insight.  The trial judge accepted Dr. Kershner’s
analysis and description of the grandparents.  It accorded with other evidence
at trial, as well as the trial judge’s own observations of them.

[
32
]

The trial judge went on to consider the weight
to be given Dr. Kershner’s report and evidence, and found as a fact that Dr.
Kershner was a well-qualified expert, her methodology was sensible and
comprehensive, and there was nothing in the evidence to support any suggestion
about bias, or unprofessional behaviour.  The evidence supports the trial
judge’s conclusions.

[
33
]

The trial judge then carefully considered both
the grandmother’s and the grandfather’s evidence.  The trial judge articulated
significant issues about the grandmother’s credibility.  She set them out
clearly.  The evidence supports her conclusions.

[
34
]

The trial judge went on to consider the
grandparents’ past parenting of the children in the context of the Society’s
earlier position that supported the grandparents’ having custody of the
children and the Society ending its involvement with the family.  The trial
judge noted that the evidence of their care of the children prior to the
assault was “confusing”.  She pointed to the discrepancy between the Society’s past
position, and its current position of seeking Crown Wardship.  She noted that
the Society’s reaction to the assault, in the context of the grandparents’ past
care of the children could be viewed as either an over response to an isolated
incident, or “a cautionary tale about inadequate supervision.”  The trial judge
concluded, on the basis of all the evidence, that it was the latter; namely the
Society had not adequately supervised the grandparents while the children were
in their care.

[
35
]

In looking at this issue, the trial judge
carefully considered the evidence of the parental support worker, who had
worked with the grandparents prior to the assault.  She had significant
concerns about the grandfather, in terms of his physical restraint of the
children and verbal negativity toward them.  She described grandmother as very
passive, unable to manage the children, and overwhelmed by them.  She observed
the home environment as chaotic with no rules.  The grandparents were unable to
follow through with the worker’s suggestions of how to improve matters.  The
grandfather was not amenable to any suggestions of how to improve his
parenting.

[
36
]

The trial judge also heard from two other
experts, Dr. Connie Kushnir and Dr. Vallance.  They are both psychologists.
They first tested the children shortly after their apprehension, and again in
February, 2009. They interviewed the children, and received information only
from the Society.  They did not consult with collateral sources, and did not
speak to the grandparents.  The trial judge therefore found there were some
issues around the weight to be given to these reports and their evidence.

[
37
]

Nevertheless, the trial judge accepted Dr.
Vallance’s evidence that T.C.’s initial testing placed her overall intelligence
within the extremely low range.  Dr. Vallance tested her again after she had
been in foster care for some time, and her scores had improved somewhat.  Dr.
Vallance opined that T.C. was happy with her foster family, but is conflicted
and confused because she misses her “real” family.  She was more interested,
however, in seeing her mother, rather than her grandmother.

[
38
]

D.L.1 was tested first by Dr. Kushnir and later
by Dr. Vallance.  On the first occasion, he tested as developmentally delayed.
More recently he tested within the borderline range.  He has improved
significantly since he came into care.  Dr. Vallance opined that D.L.1 sees his
foster family as his family, and does not enjoy going to the access visits.  He
needs to be reassured that his foster mother will come and get him.

[
39
]

D.L.2 currently tests in the slow
learner/borderline range.  The psychological testing describes him as “looking
for nurturance and emotional connection.”

[
40
]

The trial judge then went on to consider the
evidence of the access supervisors in terms of their descriptions of the
grandparents’ interactions with the children.  The grandparents had weekly
supervised access visits with the children from shortly after the children were
apprehended until the time of trial.  What was of particular concern to the
trial judge was the access supervisors’ evidence that the grandparents “were
unable to learn new parenting skills in order to improve their ability to
support the children in improving their behaviour.”
[8]

[
41
]

The trial judge then articulated the “real issues”
in the case relating to the grandparents as:

(a)

Whether the grandparents’ parenting skill are sufficient to allow
them to parent the children, or whether their skills are so poor as to put the
children at risk if they are returned to the grandparents;

(b)

Given the grandparents’ parenting skills, whether returning the
children to them would be in their best interests having regard to the
children's physical, mental, behavioural, educational and emotional needs and
the criteria set out in s. 37(3) of the
CFSA
; and

(c)

Whether, given the grandparents’ parenting issues, they have put
forward a plan that addresses these issues, such that placement with them would
be in the children's best interests.

[
42
]

Having reviewed all these issues, and considered
the evidence and the law, the trial judge determined that the children should
be made Crown Wards, with no access, so they can be adopted.  The foster family
with whom they have lived for three years is apparently interested in adopting
them.

Discussion:

[
43
]

The grandmother, who is the only appellant, has
set out numerous grounds of appeal.

I will attempt to deal with each
of them in turn.

Reasons unsupported by the facts and the evidence given.

[
44
]

As I have indicated above, the trial judge’s
findings of fact are overwhelmingly supported by the evidence.  I cannot
conclude she made any overriding and palpable error in this regard.

Undue weight on “the relationship between the foster
parents as against the relationship between the appellant and the children.”

[
45
]

The trial judge is required under the
CFSA
to
consider both the relationship of the children with the foster parents, as well
as their relationship with the appellant.  As the finder of facts, the role of
the trial judge is to ascribe the weight to be given to each aspect of the
evidence.  She did so in a completely balanced fashion.  I cannot conclude she
gave undue weight to the children’s relationship with the foster parents.

Failure to properly evaluate the method adopted by Dr.
Betty Kershner

[
46
]

As I have set out above, the trial judge
carefully considered Dr. Kershner’s methodology.  The doctor was cross-examined
vigorously about her methodology and her failure to interview various other
collaterals.  Dr. Kershner was clear in her explanation of why it was not
necessary for her purposes to do so.  It is noteworthy that Dr. Kershner was
retained on the consent of the parties.  Dr. Kershner indicated on
cross-examination that she would have interviewed collaterals if she had been
asked to do so.  She was not.  The appellant cannot now complain about that.

Dismissive nature of the other expert reports

[
47
]

Dr. Vallance and Dr. Kushnir are both
psychologists.  Between the two of them, they performed psychological
assessments of all three children in November of 2007 and again in February of
2009.  While the trial judge made some negative comments about these experts,
in terms of both the foundational information each had relied on, and Dr.
Vallance’s failure to bring her clinical notes, the trial judge nevertheless
accepted a great number of their findings.  It is noteworthy that these
assessments focused on the children, since they were designed in large part to
help the schools plan for appropriate educational programmes for the children,
since each of them was determined to have extremely low cognitive skills.

[
48
]

Although the reports make reference to
information from the foster mother, they do not opine on the suitability of
either the foster family or the grandparents as an appropriate placement for
the children.  I cannot conclude that the trial judge was either dismissive of
these expert reports, or gave them insufficient weight.  Indeed, her findings
confirm, in large part, the findings of these two experts concerning the
children’s cognitive functioning.

Dismissive nature of the video testimony of the oldest of
the children, T.C.

[
49
]

T.C. was interviewed by a police officer in the
company of a social worker just after she and her brothers were apprehended in
April 2007.  She was interviewed in order to obtain her evidence about her
grandmother’s alleged assault of one of her brothers. At the time of the
interview, T.C. had just turned 5.  Her evidence was videotaped and the disk
was made an exhibit at trial. The trial judge viewed the video and gave it
little or no weight.  I have viewed it as well, and agree completely with the
trial judge’s assessment of it.  The child’s evidence is indeed rambling and
garbled.

[
50
]

When Dr. Vallance assessed T.C. in November of
2007, she described the child as a “pleasant girl who was very talkative … However
she was very restless and in and out of her chair during most of the
assessment.  She was also impulsive and had difficulties focusing.  She asked a
lot of questions and appeared to be quite disorganized in her thoughts, speech
and her approach to tasks.  She had a difficult time understanding questions
and she asked questions that did not make sense.”

[
51
]

T.C. presented in much the same way in the
interview video.  She was six months younger at that time than she was at the
time of Dr. Vallance’s assessment.  I agree with the trial judge that T.C.’s
evidence can be given no weight at all on the issue of the grandmother’s
assault of her brother.

Misapprehension and misapplication of the videotape
evidence

[
52
]

As I have stated above, I agree with the trial
judge’s analysis and application of the videotape evidence.  I need not comment
further on this ground of appeal.

Non-recognition of the inconsistent evidence of Ms. Munoz
as regards the assault allegation/charge

[
53
]

I have already discussed the evidence of Ms.
Munoz, who was the independent witness concerning the April 2007 assault.  The
trial judge believed her evidence and disbelieved the grandmother’s evidence
concerning this event.  These conclusions were open to her on the evidence.
This ground of appeal has no merit.

The participation of the adoptive/foster parent in the
proceeding violated the rights of the Appellants in Appeal to have a hearing
which was free from bias and interference

[
54
]

Section 39(3) of the
CFSA
provides that a
foster parent who has continuously cared for a child for six months immediately
before the hearing is entitled to notice of, and to be present at the hearing.
It is common practice to have a foster parent testify.  I fail to see how their
participation can violate the appellant’s rights, or show any bias or
interference in the process.

The fact that the adoptive/foster parent was in attendance
and was permitted to give evidence at the proceedings violated the right of the
Appellant to have a hearing in the absence of the public;

[
55
]

Since the
Act
specifically authorizes the
foster parents to have notice of the proceeding, and to be present at the
hearing, there can be no violation of the appellant’s right to have a hearing
in the absence of the public.  In these circumstances, the foster parents are
not “members of the public”, but are statutorily mandated and necessary
participants in the proceedings.

The judgment placed the onus of not being involved in the
children’s life on the appellants (against the preponderance of evidence) as
opposed to the respondent;

[
56
]

Neither the appellant’s factum nor her counsel’s
argument on the appeal articulated what precisely is meant by this ground of
appeal.  I cannot conclude it has any merit.

The characterization by the trial judge of the appellants
as intellectually and emotionally limited clearly violates the principles of
fundamental justice under section 15 of the Charter

[
57
]

The trial judge’s characterization of the
appellant as intellectually and emotionally limited was overwhelmingly supported
by the evidence.  I fail to see any basis on which a factual finding such as
this could violate principles of fundamental justice under section 15 of the
Charter.

The denial of custody and/or access to the appellants
constitute a breach of their fundamental rights under section 7 of the Charter

[
58
]

Section 7 of the
Charter
guarantees
everyone the right “to life, liberty and security of the person and the right
not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of
fundamental justice.”

[
59
]

Since the
CFSA
clearly permits the court
to make a Crown Wardship order with no access, and indeed places to onus
regarding access on the party claiming it, I cannot interpret this ground of
appeal as anything other than an attack on the constitutional validity of that
section of the
CFSA.

[
60
]

If the appellant is seeking a finding that the CFSA
in providing that previous family caregivers can be denied access when a child
is made a Crown Ward is unconstitutional, I cannot deal with that ground of
appeal, since the appellant did not join the Attorney General as a party to the
appeal as required by section 109 of the
Courts of Justice Act
.

[
61
]

If, however, this ground of appeal is suggesting
that the trial judge erred in denying the grandparents access after making the
children Crown Wards, I will address it that way.

[
62
]

The trial judge correctly set out that the onus
was on the grandparents to show not only that the relationship between them and
the children was beneficial and meaningful to the children but also that access
would not impair the children’s future opportunities for adoption.

[
63
]

The trial judge found that the grandparents had
not met this onus.  She reviewed all the evidence and determined that on the
basis of the totality of the evidence “it is difficult to conclude that the
access to the children is beneficial and meaningful”.
[9]
She reached this
conclusion on the basis of all the evidence that showed the visits are
difficult for all of the children.  The grandparents lack parenting skills.
The evidence showed that none of the children has a strong attachment to their
grandparents.  These conclusions are amply supported by the evidence, as well
as the fresh evidence I admitted on the appeal.  The fresh evidence confirms
that all three of the children have little attachment to the grandparents, and
are very attached to their foster mother with whom they have now lived for
three years.

The assessments and comments of the trial judge on the
appellants were deprecatory and violated their rights under section 12 of the
Charter

[
64
]

As I have indicated above, it is not clear to me
exactly what the appellant is saying with this ground of appeal.  If there is a
suggestion that “deprecatory” comments somehow violate a person’s rights under
section 12 of the
Charter
[10]

I am completely in the dark as to what the appellant is arguing.  I was
referred to no case to support the notion that “deprecatory” remarks
constituted “cruel or unusual treatment or punishment”.

[
65
]

In any case, I cannot conclude that the trial
judge made any “deprecatory” comments about the appellant.  Her comments about
the appellant’s limitations as a parent were overwhelmingly supported by the
evidence.  I do not find her comments “deprecatory”, and even if they were, I
was referred to no authority that would suggest that deprecatory comments
violate a person’s section 12 rights.

The failure to consider that the appellants had de facto
custody of the children for almost three years, and primary care of the
children for almost two years prior to their apprehension

[
66
]

The crux of the appellant’s argument seems to be
that first, the CCAST was perfectly content with the her and the grandfather’s
caring for the children, and was prepared to terminate the Society’s involvement
with the children, and second, that a single isolated act of assault should not
be sufficient to have the Society turn around and seek the ultimate result of
removing the children, making them Crown Wards with no access so they can be
adopted, and will never see their biological family again.

[
67
]

It is true that the children had been in the
grandparents’ care for eighteen months, under supervision, and that at that
time the Society was prepared to recommend that the grandparents have custody
of the children, without ongoing Society supervision.

[
68
]

The trial judge was alive to this very issue
from the outset.  She carefully considered the issue and concluded that from
the CCAST’s point of view, with hindsight it was really a case of their not
supervising adequately in order to see the extent of the grandparents’
parenting limitations even before the children were apprehended from their
care.

[
69
]

Critical in the trial judge’s determination was
an analysis of all the evidence she heard, coupled with the affidavits of the
various support workers, and expert evidence from three psychologists.  Two,
Doctors Vallance and Kushnir were retained by CCAST to assess the children’s
cognitive development.  The third, Dr. Kershner, was retained on consent of all
the parties, to conduct a parenting capacity assessment of both the grandmother
and the grandfather.

[
70
]

The trial judge recognized that it was difficult
for the grandparents to understand why first the Society considered the
children should be place in their custody without supervision, and then should
be made Crown Wards with no access.  That said, she clearly articulated her
reasons for finding the children should be made Crown Wards.  Her conclusion is
amply supported by the totality of the evidence.

The failure to properly consider that the CCAS gave a
tacit approval for permanent placement of the children with the appellant prior
to the trial as well as their active participation and completion of parenting
classes.

[
71
]

The issue of the CCAST’s “tacit approval” to
place the children permanently with the grandparents is really the same ground
as is set out immediately above.  The court gave consideration to this fact, in
the context of all the other evidence adduced at trial.

[
72
]

Similarly, the grandparents’ completion of a
parenting course was but one piece of evidence in the totality of the
evidence.  The trial judge considered this, but accepted other evidence that
drew her to the conclusion that even with this type of support, the
grandparents were unable to parent the children, since they were and remained
unable to implement any of the suggestions they received by way of support.

Disposition:

[
73
]

For all these reasons, the grandmother’s appeal
from the finding of Crown Wardship with no access for the purpose of adoption
is dismissed.
